question: What does disease 'eradication' mean in public health?

options.A: Lowering local cases to an acceptable level
options.B: Eliminating a disease from one specific country
options.C: Permanent reduction to zero of worldwide incidence
options.D: Stopping an outbreak in a single hospital ward

explanation: You've got this! Eradication means the disease is completely wiped out across the entire globe, so we never have to fight it again. Smallpox is a great example!

question: Why must public health programs keep working even after a disease is 'eliminated' in a specific region?

options.A: To keep the pharmaceutical companies funded
options.B: Because local health workers need ongoing employment
options.C: Because the pathogen can spontaneously reform locally
options.D: To prevent re-introduction of the pathogen from other areas

explanation: Spot on! Elimination just means it's gone locally. Since it still exists in other parts of the world, travelers can easily bring it back if we drop our guard.

question: What are the three core parts of the epidemiological triangle?
explanation: Think of disease as a puzzle made of three pieces: the germ (agent), the person (host), and where they live (environment).

question: A community nurse gives out insecticide-treated bed nets to prevent malaria. Which part of the epidemiological triangle is this tackling?
explanation: Great thinking! Bed nets change the environment where humans and mosquitoes meet, keeping the vector away from you.

question: Which level of prevention covers routine childhood immunizations?
explanation: Well done! Primary prevention is all about stopping the disease before it even starts—just like vaccines do.

question: A nurse sets up a free blood pressure check at the local market. What level of prevention is this?
explanation: You nailed it! Secondary prevention is about catching health issues early through screening before they cause major trouble.

question: Which Nigerian agency leads national disease tracking and outbreak responses?

options.D: National Primary Health Care Development Agency

explanation: Spot on! The NCDC is our frontline federal agency keeping watch over public health safety across Nigeria.

question: How is 'active' surveillance different from 'passive' surveillance?

options.A: It only applies to non-communicable lifestyle diseases
options.B: Data is analyzed by artificial intelligence instead of human statisticians
options.C: Patients diagnose themselves at home using rapid test kits
options.D: Health workers go out to search for cases instead of waiting for patients to arrive

explanation: Active means taking action! Instead of waiting in the clinic, health workers actively go into communities to find hidden cases during outbreaks.

question: Why is maintaining the 'cold chain' so crucial for vaccines?

options.A: To prevent the vials from freezing solid
options.B: To preserve vaccine potency and effectiveness
options.C: To stop bacteria from growing on the outside of bottles
options.D: To make the injection less painful for infants

explanation: Exactly! Vaccines are delicate biological products. Without the proper temperature, they lose their power to protect patients.

question: Which of these is an example of 'chemoprophylaxis' in public health?

options.A: Administering the BCG vaccine to a newborn baby in the clinic
options.B: Isolating a patient with cholera in a treatment tent
options.C: Giving antimalarial medication to pregnant women to prevent malaria illness
options.D: Educating mothers on exclusive breastfeeding for six months

explanation: Chemoprophylaxis simply means using protective drugs to stop an infection before it can make a vulnerable person sick.

question: Poor waste disposal and unsafe drinking water lead directly to which group of diseases?

options.A: Genetic blood disorders like sickle cell anemia
options.B: Fecal-oral diseases like cholera and typhoid

explanation: You got it! When sanitation fails, germs from human waste easily find their way into drinking water, spreading nasty tummy bugs.

question: Why does clearing stagnant water around homes help stop disease?

options.A: It stops soil erosion during heavy rainfall
options.B: It purifies the underground water table naturally
options.C: It removes the breeding grounds for mosquito vectors
options.D: It prevents the spread of airborne tuberculosis droplets

explanation: Spot on! Mosquitoes love to lay eggs in quiet, stagnant pools. Clearing them out breaks their life cycle and keeps malaria at bay.

question: What is the main difference between isolation and quarantine?

options.A: Isolation is for chronic diseases, while quarantine is for acute injuries
options.B: Quarantine uses medications, while isolation uses physical barriers only
options.C: Isolation separates sick people, while quarantine restricts exposed healthy people
options.D: There is no difference; the terms mean the exact same thing

explanation: Easy to remember: Isolation is for those already sick, while quarantine is for healthy folks who were exposed and need to be watched.

question: During a measles outbreak, why do public health teams do 'contact tracing'?

options.A: To collect financial penalties for spreading the infection
options.B: To monitor exposed individuals during the incubation period and offer vaccination
options.C: To test the water supply for bacterial contamination
options.D: To punish individuals who failed to attend the primary health clinic

explanation: Great clinical thinking! Tracing contacts lets nurses catch infections early and vaccinate people before symptoms appear.

question: Which of these is a key frontline duty for a community health nurse in disease control?

options.A: Identifying and reporting unusual illness clusters to authorities
options.C: Managing international travel restrictions at airports
options.D: Writing national health laws in the legislative assembly

explanation: You've got this! As a nurse in the community, you are often the first to notice unusual sickness patterns and sound the alarm.

question: Why is building trust with the community so important for a nurse?

options.A: It legally protects the nurse from medical malpractice lawsuits
options.B: It encourages community members to accept immunizations and report illnesses early
options.C: It eliminates the need for any environmental sanitation work
options.D: It guarantees financial funding from international donors

explanation: Spot on! People are much more likely to listen, take their vaccines, and share health worries when they know and trust their nurse.
